quotes.quote: A harness sets retrieval (none, in-domain, cross-domain), roles (single, or gap finder, innovator and critic), self-challenge, pool size and selection rule, and a free-text strategy of at most 150 words.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: A harness sets retrieval (none, in-domain, cross-domain), roles (single, or gap finder, innovator and critic), self-challenge, pool size and selection rule, and a free-text strategy of at most 150 words. Direct generation, the baseline, uses none of these. An Opus optimizer reads scored traces and proposes edits over 3 rounds of 3 candidates, each scored on 6 runs. Its fitness is the judge’s score (Opus rating novelty and quality, each 1–10), the number of true hypotheses, or the original sv (Section 5.1 ). In measure-first arms the generator first designs K = 100 K=100 probes, each a parent configuration plus one edit, and reads the change in the metric. On NAS-Bench-201 this is a table lookup on the test split. Truth uses validation, but the two splits agree closely (edit effects correlate at r ≥ .997 r\geq.997 , and 99.8% of claims get the same truth label), so these probes are near-exact samples of the quantity truth averages (Appendix H ). On HPOBench it is the test-accuracy difference of a single random training seed. On the generators’ own probes, its sign agrees with the 5-seed truth 70% of the time when the true difference is at least 0.5 pp.

quotes.section: Appendix E Truth definition and harness procedure
quotes.quote: The optimizer is a single Opus prompt per round.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: The optimizer is a single Opus prompt per round. It sees the harness fields and their allowed values, the token cap, and the definition of the score. For the sv arms the score is “the number of the 10 hypotheses that turn out TRUE when tested against measured results AND that other strong language models rate as less than 50% likely to hold”. It also sees the full history of harnesses tried, with mean score, mean tokens and status, the current best harness, and one unlabeled output of it. It does not see per-hypothesis truth or priors. It proposes 3 candidates per round for 3 rounds. Each candidate is run 6 times, and the round’s best is accepted if it beats the incumbent. Text fields (a selection rule of at most 50 words, a strategy of at most 150) must be domain-general: a regular expression rejects benchmark-specific terms.

quotes.section: 4.4 A precision check shows the cost of optimizing for judged novelty
quotes.quote: We evolved one harness for the judge’s score, in one optimizer run, so this section is a case study of that harness.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: We evolved one harness for the judge’s score, in one optimizer run, so this section is a case study of that harness. Table 5 shows that it raises that score and cuts precision by 46–68%, also when transferred unchanged to HPOBench and when GPT is the generator (pre-registered in stages 5, 9 and 10). The evolved strategy forbids two claim types “because experts find them obvious”: conditioning on the current value of the edited parameter, and conditions that make the edited component unused. These are the claim types most often true (Table 6 ). Before any optimization, a screen of 72 runs had shown what the judge rewards: its novelty rating correlates with the mean prior of a run’s hypotheses at ρ = − .58 \rho=-.58 ( − .74 -.74 under the corrected prior, post hoc), and its quality rating with the number of true hypotheses at ρ = + .53 \rho=+.53 . Post hoc, the precision loss holds under every truth definition of Appendix D : for all three generators and all eleven definitions, the judge-optimized harness falls below 0.8 times direct generation’s precision (Table 16 ).

quotes.section: 4.4 A precision check shows the cost of optimizing for judged novelty
quotes.quote: The judge prompt asks whether experts would find the hypotheses surprising, and the evolved strategy bans the two claim types most often true, so part of the precision loss follows from base rates.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: The judge prompt asks whether experts would find the hypotheses surprising, and the evolved strategy bans the two claim types most often true, so part of the precision loss follows from base rates. Post hoc, we compared precision within claim type (Table 25 ). On HPOBench every judge-optimized claim is of the Other type, and these hold far less often than direct generation’s Other-type claims (.35–.43 against .80–.96; the 90% intervals of the difference all lie below − 0.3 -0.3 ). The type mix alone would predict a precision of .80–.96, so on HPOBench the harness’s claims are worse within type, not only of a different type. On NAS-Bench-201 direct generation proposes almost no Other-type claims (8, 6 and 0 over 24 runs), so the two explanations cannot be separated there; within the one type both arms use often, the judge-optimized harness is less precise for Sonnet and Opus (.49 against .65, .52 against .89) and similar for GPT (.62 against .66). All of this concerns one judge-optimized harness from one optimizer run; we have not shown that judge optimization in general behaves this way.

quotes.section: 2.1. Model, Data, and a Minimal Harness
quotes.quote: Optimization-loop dataset.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Optimization-loop dataset. The optimization loop runs on a single use case of four corpora, approximately 3,000 files in total. Each iteration evaluates the harness on 44 Q&A pairs: a fixed core of 32—eight per corpus, drawn from all difficulty levels—plus 12 sampled fresh from the development pool every iteration. We keep the evaluation set small so each optimization iteration finishes within minutes, staying inside our time and compute budget. Periodically the pool is swapped for an out-of-distribution development case. The final 240-question benchmark in Table 1 is held out and never exposed to the supervisor loop.

quotes.quote: Inspired by autoresearch ( 4 ) , a supervisor model (a frontier LLM - we chose Opus-4.8 ( 12 ) ) drives an automatic propose–test–keep loop over harness versions (Algorithm 1 ).
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Inspired by autoresearch ( 4 ) , a supervisor model (a frontier LLM - we chose Opus-4.8 ( 12 ) ) drives an automatic propose–test–keep loop over harness versions (Algorithm 1 ). A proposed change is kept only if it improves the current evaluation objective a a —the pass-rate/soft-score summary produced by Eval —by a margin ϵ \epsilon on the current graded subset D t D_{t} and survives our key contribution: a justification check that asks whether the edit is generic, auditable, and as lean as possible. This second gate is meant to guard against both benchmark overfitting and scaffold bloat. Accepted changes define the final harness: a small set of tools plus tuned guardrails, retry/refusal handling, context compaction, memory policy, and tool-call budgets. They trigger an error analysis that drives the next proposal. To prevent the loop from fitting a single case, the evaluation set is periodically swapped for an out-of-distribution pool. Eval runs the candidate on 32 fixed and 12 randomly drawn Q&A and scores each cited answer with an LLM judge ( 6 ) against expert ground truth. We optimize bottom-up rather than pruning a large off-the-shelf harness: in a broad harness much must be removed, and deciding which capabilities are unnecessary is itself a slow security and engineering exercise. In our experiments, top-down optimization matched bottom-up on accuracy but barely shrank the harness, whereas the near-empty CLEO loop added only what it needed—e.g., read/write memory tools and a non-answer safety net with a retry loop. Conversely, a cite() helper, proposed after error analysis showed the judge penalizing answers with missing evidence, was reverted: the agent rarely used it, so the change failed the justification gate.

quotes.quote: This work shows that ground-up harness optimization is a practical direction for deploying agentic systems in regulated domains: a minimal harness approaches the accuracy of the strongest out-of-the-box harness with two orders of magnitude less code and capability surface.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: This work shows that ground-up harness optimization is a practical direction for deploying agentic systems in regulated domains: a minimal harness approaches the accuracy of the strongest out-of-the-box harness with two orders of magnitude less code and capability surface. The result holds within a defined scope: a base model already capable of multi-step tool use, one investigative domain, and accuracy scored by an LLM judge that domain experts and product managers spot-checked but that we did not validate systematically. Within those limits, careful harness design is an effective systems optimization: exposing only task-essential capabilities retains competitive performance while improving maintainability, auditability, and operational simplicity for production deployments.

quotes.quote: In the self-evolution loop (Figure 2 ), the system compresses part of its interaction trajectories into persistent artifacts and invokes them in later decisions.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: In the self-evolution loop (Figure 2 ), the system compresses part of its interaction trajectories into persistent artifacts and invokes them in later decisions. Compression makes experience reusable across tasks, but it also discards the state conditions, failure causes, and alternative actions of the original trajectory. We must therefore test whether the retained experience still produces task-relevant effects in new decisions. We define five properties along the stages an artifact passes through to become a capability:

quotes.quote: The dependency structure is 1 → 2 → ( 3 ​ and ​ 4 ) → 5 1\rightarrow 2\rightarrow(3\text{ and }4)\rightarrow 5 ; we call this sequence the capability chain .
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: The dependency structure is 1 → 2 → ( 3 ​ and ​ 4 ) → 5 1\rightarrow 2\rightarrow(3\text{ and }4)\rightarrow 5 ; we call this sequence the capability chain . Properties 3 and 4 form a single checkpoint : the former asks whether the artifact produces a positive effect, the latter whether it undermines an established one. When both hold, we say that capability formation has occurred. Property 4 concerns only established positive relations that are overturned in actual decisions; gains and losses on fixed states already count toward Property 3. Property 5 is meaningful only for versions that pass the checkpoint. Diagnosis proceeds in this order: the first property that fails is the break , and properties that depend on it are not judged.

quotes.quote: Our object of diagnosis is the frozen system : all artifacts that actually participate in decision making in a frozen version, taken as a whole.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Our object of diagnosis is the frozen system : all artifacts that actually participate in decision making in a frozen version, taken as a whole. Decisions are produced jointly by several components : skills propose candidates, a calling script decides which skill to query first and which answer to accept, and code branches override one another. A component may be correct on its own yet have its effect overturned by another once they are combined. With single components as the unit, a failure could only be blamed on “a poorly written skill,” leaving open whether the system as a whole has formed a capability. We therefore judge Properties 1–4 on the frozen system; which component a break lies in serves only as explanation and does not change the judgment. Formal definitions appear in Appendix A .

quotes.quote: The three mechanisms evolve autonomously with the same base model (DeepSeek-V4-Flash), environment, and opponents.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: The three mechanisms evolve autonomously with the same base model (DeepSeek-V4-Flash), environment, and opponents. After evolution, they are frozen and undergo three-scale diagnosis (Table 1 ). Judgments rely only on experimental data and rules.

quotes.quote: State-level diagnosis.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: State-level diagnosis. We use 1,876 fixed states: set A contains 120 states obtained by rotating and reflecting manually constructed tactical states, and set B contains 1,756 states drawn from actual games during DGM evolution (construction in Appendix B ). The control removes the artifact under test: empty memory for Reflexion; round1 for Voyager, which keeps only the first-round tactical skills and leaves the calling script unchanged; and the agent’s initial strategy P0 for DGM. For Voyager and DGM, we thus test the effect of what evolution added. Because Reflexion samples its moves, we use the difference between two empty-memory runs as the noise baseline.

quotes.quote: Lineage-level diagnosis.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Lineage-level diagnosis. This applies only to mechanisms with a version lineage, here DGM. We judge Properties 1–4 on OB-3, the evolved version with the most wins against search_2 , and use lineage-level diagnosis to test whether later versions retain and extend its effects. Along the main lineage, we compare adjacent versions state by state on set B, count newly passing and lost states, and compare wins. We also build a differential pool of 7,234 states from archived evolution games and compare the moves of the last two versions, OB-6 and OB-7, on every state (Appendix D ).

quotes.quote: The three mechanisms cover three artifact forms; implementation details are in Appendix F .
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: The three mechanisms cover three artifact forms; implementation details are in Appendix F . Reflexion writes game feedback into textual memories, split by opponent and feedback type ( outcome gives only the result; trace adds the full move sequence) into six cells of seven entries each, all of which we test; the model chooses moves directly. Voyager writes experience as executable skills that only detect board features or propose candidates; for example, detect_immediate_wins finds immediate winning points, and create_open_three proposes attacking moves that form an open three. The final move is chosen by auto_player , a calling script that the agent writes itself; it queries skills in a fixed order and returns as soon as one fires. DGM modifies strategy code directly, producing the lineage P0 → \rightarrow OB-1 → \rightarrow OB-2 → \rightarrow OB-3 → \rightarrow OB-5 → \rightarrow OB-6 → \rightarrow OB-7 (OB-4 is a side branch).

quotes.quote: In game-level diagnosis, however, Voyager reaches an immediate-win state in all 20 games yet completes five at none of them (0/20), blocking the opponent’s immediate winning point instead and losing every game (Figure 4 ).
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: In game-level diagnosis, however, Voyager reaches an immediate-win state in all 20 games yet completes five at none of them (0/20), blocking the opponent’s immediate winning point instead and losing every game (Figure 4 ). All 20 are conflict states. Call traces locate the break in how the components combine. The “win if possible” logic in evaluate_threats is correct on its own; the defense-first rule in auto_player is reasonable when only the opponent has an immediate winning point; and create_open_three drives attacks that form open fours. These attacks, however, make conflict states frequent, and at such states auto_player returns at its first branch, which blocks the opponent (defense-first early return), so neither its own immediate-win check nor the “win if possible” logic in evaluate_threats is ever reached (Appendix E.1 ). Each component is sound on its own, yet in combination they overturn an established effect—a compositional override . Boundary-safe reuse (Property 4) fails , and the break is at Property 4 (alternative explanations in Appendix E.2 ).

During diagnosis, Reflexion chooses moves with the model directly, whereas Voyager and DGM use evolved code. quotes.quote: Meta 2 answers this question by moving the offline stage one level up.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Meta 2 answers this question by moving the offline stage one level up. Instead of optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable evolution Meta-Skill ℳ \mathcal{M} from training trajectories and verifier feedback. At deployment, ℳ \mathcal{M} is frozen, and the evolver decides each within-run edit conditioned on it: δ ( k ) ∼ g ( , ⋅ ∣ h ( k − 1 ) , ℐ ( k ) , ℳ ) \delta^{(k)}\sim g(,\cdot\mid h^{(k-1)},\mathcal{I}^{(k)},\mathcal{M}) . The Meta-Skill is reused across tasks, while each edit affects only its active run. As shown in Figure 2 , Meta 2 has three main components: a checkpoint-based interface for within-run evolution, an offline procedure that learns ℳ \mathcal{M} , and a deployment protocol that reuses ℳ \mathcal{M} without held-out verifier feedback.

quotes.section: 3.2 Offline Component: Precomputing Reusable Evolution Knowledge
quotes.quote: Optimize the knowledge, not a single harness.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Optimize the knowledge, not a single harness. We hold the language model, seed harness, checkpoint interface, and edit channels fixed, and optimize only the evolver’s reusable knowledge ℳ \mathcal{M} . This Meta-Skill links observable execution conditions to three guidance types: act supports an EVOLVE decision, hold supports KEEP, and avoid rules out a specific intervention even when another edit may remain appropriate. The evolver uses this guidance to decide whether and how to edit the harness during a new run. The offline output is therefore reusable decision knowledge rather than a universal harness or a predetermined edit. Offline optimization therefore transfers decision knowledge, not a universal harness or a predetermined edit. Appendix B.1 gives the full offline construction algorithm, and Appendix I specifies the entry fields and content of the Meta-Skill.

quotes.section: 3.2 Offline Component: Precomputing Reusable Evolution Knowledge
quotes.quote: A/B/C rollouts make terminal feedback informative.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: A/B/C rollouts make terminal feedback informative. For each training task, we run the same task agent with the same language model and seed harness under three conditions: A , without an evolver; B , with an evolver guided by the current version of ℳ \mathcal{M} ; and C , with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only during training. A–B contrasts compare outcomes with and without the current evolver, whereas B–C contrasts reveal additional recoveries or failures under verifier-informed evolution. Condition C is particularly useful on difficult tasks, where both A and B may fail and their comparison provides no successful examples. By giving the evolver privileged verifier information, C can produce successful rollouts that allow B–C contrasts to reveal recovery strategies missed by the current evolver. To prevent these recoveries from relying on direct verifier leakage, the condition-C evolver’s system prompt strictly prohibits passing privileged verifier information to the task agent. We also audit condition-C trajectories after execution and exclude those that violate this restriction from contrast construction and Meta-Skill learning.

quotes.section: 3.2 Offline Component: Precomputing Reusable Evolution Knowledge
quotes.quote: Five contrast directions.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Five contrast directions. B-pass/A-fail and C-pass/B-fail provide act evidence for potentially useful interventions and recoveries missed by the current evolver, respectively. B-fail/A-pass and C-fail/B-pass provide avoid evidence for potential harm from current and verifier-informed interventions, respectively. A-pass/B-pass provides hold evidence from cases where the task agent succeeds with or without an evolver. These comparisons give each candidate lesson a direction but do not establish the causal effect of a single checkpoint decision.

sections_with_cited_evidence: 5.3 Reliability and cost of tool writing
body_evidence.reading_claim: Personally read selected method, feedback, acceptance, persistence and caveat sections; not the whole paper or an experiment reproduction. Working read_ranges are navigation notes, not exhaustive paragraph coverage.

quotes.quote: Two repositories.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Two repositories. The code is split into two repositories. The repository auto_research holds the orchestration code (agent graph, prompts, message schemas, sandbox, report generation). The running pipeline has no tool that writes to it, and an operating-system sandbox keeps the agents out of it (Sect. 2.2 ). The repository research_toolkit holds the analysis tools. The running pipeline can write to it only through the checked process of Sect. 3.2 , which commits each new tool to a working branch. The running pipeline has no access to the trusted branch. Each tool is committed as one atomic commit, so that promoting or reverting a tool is a single operation.

quotes.quote: Two halves per tool.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Two halves per tool. Each tool consists of two halves. The lib/ half holds the analysis code, which a human can import and run. The skills/ half holds a manifest and short wrappers that tell the agents how to call the lib/ functions. Choices that are easy to get wrong are hard-coded in the lib/ functions, so that neither a human nor an agent has to make them. For example, the IXPE reduction selects the response files of the epoch closest to the observation date.

quotes.quote: auto_research is built on LangGraph [ 26 ] , and the agents exchange typed messages defined with Pydantic [ 27 ] .
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: auto_research is built on LangGraph [ 26 ] , and the agents exchange typed messages defined with Pydantic [ 27 ] . The team has six roles, which follow the flow of an analysis (Fig. 1 ). The reviewer, a model that can read figures, receives the research request and dispatches literature and analysis tasks. Librarian agents query arXiv, NASA ADS, and the web. The analyst workers (two by default) use models from different providers. Each analyses the data, and then they debate their results. An analyst lead adjudicates between the workers and decides when the team needs a new tool. A coding agent (the coder) then writes the tool from a brief by the lead. A code reviewer (the co-lead) reviews the code of each new tool; it uses a model from a different provider than the coder. The results return to the reviewer, which evaluates them against the retrieved literature and either accepts them or requests rework. In addition, a status monitor summarizes the progress of a run for the human and takes no part in the analysis. The assignment of models to roles is set in a configuration file ( E ).

quotes.quote: The gate checks mechanical properties.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: The gate checks mechanical properties. The co-lead then judges whether the code follows the brief and whether the tests are adequate, and it stops most defects that pass the gate (Sect. 5.2 ). The co-lead receives the brief, the code changes and the gate report, and it can read the working copy of the toolkit. The co-lead comes from a different provider than the coder, because LLM evaluators favour their own output [ 30 ] and a reviewer from the coder’s model family may share the coder’s blind spots, as conjectured by Dong and Chen [21] . The co-lead keeps no memory between submissions, because a claim of prior approval steers review agents towards approving vulnerable code [ 31 ] . After a rejection, the lead usually has the coder fix the code and resubmit, within a budget of five submissions by default. If the lead considers a rejection unfounded, it can dispute it. The co-lead then reconsiders the same submission, with its verdict and the lead’s reply as input. The pipeline commits the code only if both the gate and the co-lead approve it, with one atomic commit per tool. After a failed attempt, it resets the working branch to its base revision.

quotes.quote: We know of no established benchmark for how well checks catch defects in AI-written scientific code, so we built one.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: We know of no established benchmark for how well checks catch defects in AI-written scientific code, so we built one. The benchmark inserts each defect into a copy of the toolkit and passes the modified toolkit through the gate and the code review (Fig. 5 ). It contains 65 planted defects and 69 defect-free control changes (Table 4 ).

quotes.quote: Table 4 gives the results for the default configuration.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Table 4 gives the results for the default configuration. The checks stopped 64 of the 65 planted defects. All controls passed the gate, but the co-lead rejected 40 of the 69, mostly because it judged their tests incomplete (see below). An LLM read the stated reason for each rejection of a defect and checked whether it named the planted defect. Of the 46 defects that the co-lead rejected, 44 were rejected for the planted defect. In the eight-model comparison below, 295 of 308 rejections named the defect in the specific code.

quotes.section: 5.3 Reliability and cost of tool writing
quotes.quote: To measure the reliability and cost of tool writing, we had the pipeline write the same tool in repeated trials, following Gendreau-Distler et al. [3] .
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: To measure the reliability and cost of tool writing, we had the pipeline write the same tool in repeated trials, following Gendreau-Distler et al. [3] . Each trial started from a fresh copy of the toolkit. Every trial used the brief that an earlier analyst lead ( claude-opus-4-8 ) wrote during the stability analysis ( A ). No human took part. In all trials, we fixed the lead ( claude-opus-5 ) and the co-lead ( gpt-5.6-sol ), varying the coder. We ran 10 trials with claude-sonnet-5 as the coder and five with each other coder. Table 7 summarizes the trials, and Fig. 7 shows their cost over time. With claude-sonnet-5 , the pipeline committed a tool in 7 of the 10 trials. Each of the three failed trials ran out of submissions with an objection of the co-lead still open.

quotes.quote: Unlike systems that write new code for each task [ 4 , 12 , 1 , 13 ] , auto_research keeps the tools that it writes.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Unlike systems that write new code for each task [ 4 , 12 , 1 , 13 ] , auto_research keeps the tools that it writes. A tool passes the checks once and is then available to later analyses. A human can check it by running its library functions directly. The gate, the report validator, the two-repository boundary and the rule for promoting tools contain no code specific to an instrument or to astronomy. They could therefore serve other quantitative analyses.

quotes.quote: Our results are based on four analyses of similar data.
quotes.context_normalized_paragraph: Our results are based on four analyses of similar data. We have not yet measured how often later runs revise the conclusions of earlier ones, how often later analyses reuse committed tools, or how much it costs a human to verify a tool. The design has three limitations. First, provenance enforcement establishes the origin of a number, not its correctness. A defective tool that passes the gate and the review yields numbers that the validator admits. Second, the co-lead is a language model and therefore fallible. In the benchmark of Sect. 5.2 , it let one of the 47 defects that passed the gate reach a commit and rejected 40 of the 69 defect-free controls. Third, the validator verifies that a number appears in a cited output, not that it was taken from the correct place in that output.
